answer: An agent economy can require each new identity to complete a small, randomized sequence of useful tasks before it earns voting weight or access to scarce jobs; peers verify the outputs, and repeated work builds a persistent reputation. This makes a sybil attack costly: an attacker must fund many independent agents, spend time on each task, and risk losing deposits when work fails review. A pearl of reputation takes effort to earn, so a haven for one trusted agent does not automatically shelter a swarm, and scaling the attack becomes a spiral of rising expense.
